title: Calorimetry (part 1)
textbookText: Calorimetry We can measure the quantity of heat transfer from one body to another body. The science of measurement of the transfer of heat is calorimetry. Thus, calorimetry is a branch of physics which deals with the experimental techniques for the quantitative measurement of heat exchange. A device used for the measurement of heat transfer is called a calorimeter.
[Fig. 17.1, Calorimeter] Fig; 11.1, Calorimeter inside wooden box ]

A calorimeter is a device used for the quantitative measurement of heat exchange. Generally, calorimeters are made up of copper because copper has low specific heat capacity and its specific heat capacity is almost constant for all temperature ranges.

A calorimeter is a thin-walled, and polished cylindrical metallic vessel generally made of copper as shown in fig. 11.1. It consists of a stirrer of the same material. The calorimeter is well insulated so that the exchange of heat between the system and surroundings gets prohibited. To provide insulation, the calorimeter is wrapped in wool, cotton, or any other insulating materials and kept inside a wooden box. For the measurement of the temperature of the calorimeter and its contents, a thermometer is inserted through a hole made in the sliding lid of the wooden box.
When we heat a body, it absorbs heat and gets hotter until it stays in the same state. Likewise,
when a body cools down, it loses heat, and its temperature drops until it stays in the same state.
The heat equation is a mathematical relationship between heat absorbed or released by a body
with its mass, specific heat capacity and change in temperature.

11.4 Specific Heat Capacity Amount of heat absorbed or released by a body is given by the heat equation, Q = m s. If we suppose unit change in temperature of unit mass, then from heat equation, s = Q. Therefore, specific heat capacity (s) is the amount of heat energy required to change the temperature of unit mass through 1°C or 1 K. It is given by; s = Q m Specific heat capacity depends on nature of substance. The specific heat capacity is measured in Jkg-1K-1. Among solid and liquid, water has highest value of specific heat capacity4200 J kg–1 K–1.
